div.p: The proof of your ignorance, which by the very act of defending injustice convicts it, is plain enough: that all who once shared your ignorance and your hatred, the moment it falls to them to know, cease to hate as soon as they cease to be ignorant; indeed, they become the very thing they hated and begin to hate what they once were. Every day you groan over the growing number of Christians; you cry out that the city is under siege; you complain that in the fields, in the forts, on the islands there are Christians, that every sex, every age, every rank is going over to us, as though it were a loss to you. And yet not even by this do you raise your minds to suspect some hidden good. You are not permitted to suspect more rightly, you have no wish to test the matter more closely; here alone human curiosity grows numb. You love to be ignorant of what others rejoice to have found; you would rather not know, because you already hate, as though you were quite certain you would not hate once you knew. But if no hatred is owed, surely the best course will be to withdraw from your earlier injustice; while if a real cause stands firm, nothing will be taken from your hatred, which will rather be heaped higher by the awareness of its justice. Unless it is shame that keeps you from amending, or distaste that keeps you from being excused. I know well the answer with which you usually meet the testimony of our growth. The good of a thing, you say, is not to be inferred from the mere fact that it converts many and sweeps them to itself. I am familiar with the mind's change for the worse. How many deserters from the good life? How many turncoats to perversity? Many in good faith, indeed by now more of them on account of the extremities of the times. But the comparison you draw breaks down in its equivalence. For evil is so established in the judgment of all that not even the guilty themselves, who go over to evil and turn aside from good things into perverse ones, dare to defend evil as if it were good. They count base things matter for fear, impious things matter for shame. In short, they long to lie hidden, they shun appearing, they tremble when caught, they deny when accused; not even under torture do they confess easily or always, and once condemned they certainly grieve. They reproach themselves with what they were, they attribute the mind's evil passage from innocence to fate. So unwilling are they to own it as theirs, because they cannot deny it is evil. But the Christian, what such thing does he undergo? No one is ashamed, no one repents, except only of his former life. If he is denounced, he glories; if he is dragged to court, he does not resist; if he is accused, he makes no defense; questioned, he confesses; condemned, he gives thanks. What sort of evil is this, in which the very nature of evil is absent?

Now our defense demands that we engage with you, pitiable nations, concerning your gods, summoning your own conscience to judge whether they are truly gods, as you would have it, or falsely, as you are unwilling to know. For this is the matter of human error, through its very contriver, so that ignorance may not be free of error, that you may be the more guilty for it. The eyes are open, yet they do not see; the ears gape, yet they do not hear; the heart, throbbing, is dull; the mind does not know what it acknowledges. In short, if it were permitted to dispel so great a perversity by a single prescription, the announcement would be ready at hand: since we know that all these gods were instituted by men, the trust in their true divinity already collapses on this very ground, that nothing which once had a beginning can by any right be seen as divine. But there are many things by which the tenderness of conscience is hardened into the callousness of voluntary error. The truth is besieged by a vast host, and is itself secure in its own power! Why not? She takes to herself as allies and protectors, from the very adversaries, whomever she wishes, and lays low all that whole multitude of besiegers. Against these, then, our task lies — against the institutions of forefathers, the authorities of those received, the laws of those who rule, the argumentations of the prudent; against antiquity, custom, necessity; against examples, portents, miracles, all of which have fortified that counterfeit divinity. Wherefore, following your own commentaries, which you have taken from every kind of theology, joining the contest step by step — since in such matters the authority of writings is greater among you than that of facts — I have chosen, for the sake of brevity, the works of Varro, who, having commented on divine matters out of all that has been arranged before, has set himself out to us as a suitable mark. If I question him, he points out as introducers of the gods either philosophers or peoples or poets. For he distinguished the reckoning of the gods into a threefold kind: one physical, which the philosophers handle; another mythical, which is tossed about among the poets; the third national, which each people has adopted for itself. Therefore, since the philosophers have contrived the physical by conjectures, the poets have drawn the mythical from fables, and the peoples have presumed the national of their own accord, where, then, is the truth to be placed? In conjectures? But the conception is uncertain. In fables? But the account is foul. In adoptions? But the adoption is haphazard and parochial. In short, among the philosophers it is uncertain, because various; among the poets all unworthy, because base; among the peoples all haphazard, because arbitrary. But divinity, if you examine the true one, is of such a definition that it can neither be gathered by uncertain argumentations, nor be contaminated by unworthy fables, nor be judged by haphazard adoptions; for it ought to be held, as it is, certain, entire, common, because of course it belongs to all. But what god am I to believe? The one whom suspicion has guessed at? The one whom history has bandied about? The one whom the city has willed? Far more worthily would I believe none than one that is dubious, or shameful, or adopted.

In this matter you yourselves pass judgment against the very form by which the wicked are judged. For when the guilty are brought before you, if they deny the charge, you press them with tortures to confession; but Christians, when they have confessed of their own accord, you crush with tortures to make them deny. What perversity is this, that you resist confession, that you reverse the office of torture, forcing the prisoner to escape acquitted, to deny against his will? Magistrates appointed to wring out the truth, from us alone you demand a lie, that we should say we are not what we are. I suppose you do not want us to be evil men, and so you are eager to shut us out from this name. Certainly you torture all the rest to make them deny that they are what they are charged with being. Yet when those others deny, you do not believe them; us, if we deny, you believe at once. If you are certain that we are utterly criminal, why even in this are we treated by you otherwise than the criminal? I do not say that you allow no room either for accusation or for defense — though you are accustomed not rashly to condemn the unaccused and undefended. But for instance: when a case is brought against a murderer, the cause is not settled, nor inquiry satisfied, the moment he has confessed to the name of murderer. Indeed, even when men confess you find it hard to believe them; you go further and require the attendant circumstances: how often he committed the killing, with what weapons, in what places, with what spoils, accomplices, harborers, so that nothing at all of the bad man's deed may lie hidden, nor anything be lacking to the truth that must be built up toward the sentence. But concerning us, whom you charge with more atrocious and more numerous crimes, you draw up briefer and lighter indictments. I suppose you do not want them burdened whom you want ruined by every means, or you think there is no need to inquire into what you already know. This then is the more perverse, if you compel men to deny things of which you are most certainly informed. Indeed, the more it suited your hatred — setting aside the proper form of judging, by your own zeal — not to strive for denial, lest you should free those you hate, but for the confession of each crime, so that your enmity might be the more gorged by the heaping up of penalties: while it was being established how many of those banquets each had already celebrated, how often in the dark he had rushed upon incest. What of this? That, in order to root out the breed, the investigation ought to have been spread wide, the inquiry extended to accomplices and the privy. Let the child-purveyors and the cooks be produced, the very dogs that draw the lights — the case would have been completed. Then would entertainment be added for the spectacle. With how much zeal would men crowd into the arena when some man was about to fight to the death who had devoured a hundred infants! For if such horrible and monstrous things are reported of us, surely they ought to have been brought to light, lest they seem incredible and the public hatred of us cool. For most people temper their belief in such things, shuddering to seek as a beast's food the kind which it has barred itself from by intercourse with the human race.

But the authority of the physicist philosophers patronizes itself as the bondservant of wisdom. To be sure, the pure wisdom of philosophers — whose feebleness is first attested by this very variety of opinions, which comes from ignorance of the truth. But what wise man is without truth, who is ignorant of God, the father and lord of that very wisdom and truth? For there is also the divine pronouncement of Solomon elsewhere: "The beginning of wisdom," he says, "is the fear of God." Now the origin of fear is knowledge; for who will fear what he does not know? Thus he who has feared God, when he is more known than all, having attained the knowledge and truth of the God of all, will obtain full and perfect wisdom. But this has not clearly fallen to philosophy. For although, through the curiosity of inspecting literature of every kind, they may seem to have run also into the divine scriptures, as the more ancient, and thence to have drawn off something, yet when they have interpolated it, they prove that they have either despised everything or not believed everything — for in other matters too the simplicity of truth wavers through the scrupulosity of a haphazard faith — and so, with the lust for glory added to the works of their own genius, they changed it, whereby even what they had found passed into uncertainty, and from one or another drip of truth there was made a flood of argumentations. For having found God in name only, they did not set him forth as they had found him, but so as to dispute about his quality and his nature, even about his abode: the Platonists, indeed, making him caring for things and arbiter and judge; the Epicureans, idle and unexercised and, so to speak, nobody; placed outside the world by the Stoics, within the world by the Platonists. Him whom they had not thoroughly admitted, they could neither know nor fear, nor thence be wise — straying, of course, from the beginning of wisdom, that is, the fear of God. There exist testimonies of a divinity as much unknown as doubted among the philosophers. Diogenes, consulted as to what is done in the heavens: "I have never," he said, "gone up." Likewise, asked whether there are gods: "I do not know," he said, "except that it would be expedient that there should be." Thales of Miletus, to Croesus inquiring what he thought about the gods, after several leaves of deliberation, replied, "Nothing." Socrates himself denied those gods, as if certain. The same man ordered a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius, as if certain. And therefore, since philosophy is found so uncertain and inconstant in defining about God, what fear could it have of one whom it could not clearly hold to define? Of the world as god we have learned. For this the physical kind of theology forces, since they have so handed down the gods that Dionysius the Stoic divides them three ways. He would have one species which is in plain sight, like the Sun, the Moon, the Stars; another which does not appear, like Neptune; the rest which is said to have passed from men to divinity, like Hercules, Amphiaraus. Likewise Arcesilaus draws a threefold form of divinity: the Olympians, the Stars, the Titans, from Heaven and Earth: of these, from Saturn and Ops, Neptune, Jupiter and Orcus, and the rest of the succession. Xenocrates the Academic makes it two ways: the Olympians and the Titans, who are from Heaven and Earth. Most of the Egyptians believe in four gods: the Sun and the Moon, the Heaven and the Earth. Democritus supposes the gods to have arisen, with the rest, from the upper fire — of which sort Zeno would have nature be. Whence Varro too makes fire the soul of the world, so that fire likewise governs all things in the world, just as the soul in us. But most emptily. For when it is in us, he says, we are ourselves; when it has gone out, we die. Therefore fire too, when it departs from the world through the lightning-flashes, the world dies.

You then, on other occasions most diligent and persistent investigators of crimes far smaller, when faced with such horrors as these, surpassing every impiety, abandon that diligence — neither accepting the confession, which judges should always labor over, nor sorting out the examination, which prosecutors should always attend to. From this it is now plain that the whole charge against us is directed not at any crime, but at a name. For if it rested on the truth of crimes, the very names of the crimes would be enough to condemn us, if they were applied; so that the pronouncement against us would run thus: "It is decreed that that man, a murderer, or guilty of incest, or whatever we are charged with, be led off, be crucified, be thrown to the beasts." But your sentences brand nothing except the confession of being a Christian. No name of a crime exists, unless the name itself is the crime. This is in truth the whole basis of the hatred against us. The name is at issue, against which a certain hidden power makes war through your ignorance, so that you are unwilling to know for certain what you are certain you do not know for certain; and therefore you neither believe what is not proved, and, lest it be readily disproved, you are unwilling to inquire, so that the hated name may be punished on the presumption of crimes. Indeed, so that we may be released from the hated name, we are forced to deny it; and then, denying it, we are set free, with full impunity for all that is past — no longer murderers nor guilty of incest, because we have lost that name. But while this reasoning is shown in its place, declare what it is you pursue to the destruction of the name: what is the crime of the name, what the offense, what the fault? For it is laid down against you that you cannot bring charges which no established law assigns, no formal indictment fixes, no sentence enumerates. What is laid before the magistrate, what is inquired into concerning the accused, what is answered or denied, what is read out from the council's record — that I acknowledge as belonging to a defendant. And so, as to the merit of a name, if there is any guilt in names, any accusation in words, I think there is no quarrel with a word or a name unless it either sounds barbarous, or smacks of ill omen, or is obscene, or is otherwise than befits the speaker or pleases the hearer. Such are the faults of words or names, just as in expressions and discourse a barbarism is a defect, and a solecism, and a clumsy figure. But the Christian name, so far as its meaning goes, is interpreted from "anointing." Even when you mispronounce it as "Chrestiani" — for you are not even clearly certain of the name itself — it is still shaped from sweetness or goodness. You hold fast then, in harmless men, even our harmless name, which is no hardship to the tongue, not harsh to the ears, not evil to man, not hostile to the country, but both Greek, like others, and pleasant in sound and in interpretation. And surely names are not to be punished by sword or cross or beasts.

These matters thus dispatched, we see that this physical reckoning is suborned to contend that the elements are gods, while it also alleges that from these other gods too are born; for gods could be born only from gods. Whom, since we shall examine them more fully in their place among the poets in the mythical, yet — what for the moment must be retracted concerning them, so far as makes for the present species — we shall perhaps show, turning at once from the present species to them, that those said to be born of the elements can in no way be seen to be gods; so that it may now hence be prejudged that the elements are not gods, since those said to be born of the elements are not gods; equally, demonstrating that the elements are not gods, we shall build up beforehand, against that species of kindred gods, that they are rightly defended as not gods whose parents, that is, the elements, are not gods. It is settled that a god is born of a god, just as of a non-god a non-god. Therefore, since this world contains the elements — to treat summarily of the whole, as supplying its parts (for whatever its condition is, the same surely will be that also of the elements and members) — it must either have been instituted by someone, as Plato's humaneness has it, or by no one, as Epicurus's hardness has it; and if it was instituted, having a beginning it will also have an end. Thus what once was not before its beginning, and at some time will not be after its end, surely cannot be seen as a god, lacking the substance of divinity, that is, eternity, which is reckoned to be without beginning and end. But if it was not instituted at all, and is therefore to be held a god, because as a god it suffers neither beginning nor end of itself — how do some assign to the elements, which they would have to be gods, a generation, when the Stoics deny that anything is born to a god? Again, how do they wish those whom they report to be born of the elements to be held gods, when they deny that a god is born? And so what belongs to the world, this will be ascribed to the elements — I mean to heaven and earth and the stars and fire — which Varro has proposed to you, in vain, to be believed gods and parents of gods, against the denial of generation and birth in a god; as the same Varro had indicated that heaven and the stars are animate beings. But if this is so, they must also be mortal, according to the form of an animate being; for although it is settled that the soul is immortal, this will be lawful only for it, not also for that to which it is joined, that is, the body. But no one will deny that the elements have a body, since we both touch them and are touched by them, and we see certain bodies fall away from them. Therefore, if they are animate beings, the reckoning of the soul set aside, by the condition of bodies, they are mortal, surely not immortal. And yet, whence do the elements seem to Varro to be animate beings? Because the elements move. And lest it be objected from the other side that many other things move, like wheels, like wagons, like other machines, he forestalls it of his own accord, saying that they were believed animate because they move of themselves, no mover or rouser of them appearing from without, as appears one who drives the wheel and turns the wagon and works the machine. Therefore, unless they are animate, they are not movable of themselves. But, alleging what does not appear, he shows what he ought to have sought, that is, an artificer and arbiter of the motion; for a thing is not at once nonexistent which, because we do not see it, we do not believe to exist. Rather, all the more highly is that to be investigated which is not seen, that we may be able to know of what sort is that which is seen. Otherwise, if only those things which are visible are believed to exist because they are visible, how do you receive as gods even those who are not visible? But if those seem to exist who do not exist, why should not those exist also who are not seen? I mean a mover of the heavenly things. Let them be animate beings, then, because they are movable of themselves; even movable of themselves, because not by another; yet so that they are not at once gods because animate, nor for this reason, that they are movable of themselves. Or what forbids that all animate beings, as movable of themselves, be held gods? And this indeed, by another vanity, the Egyptians are free to do.

But you say the sect is punished by the name of its founder. First, that a sect should be marked by the appellation of its founder is, of course, an honest and customary right, since philosophers too are surnamed from their founders, as Pythagoreans and Platonists, as physicians the Erasistratians and grammarians the Aristarchians. Therefore, if on account of an evil founder a sect is evil, it is punished as the transmission of an evil name. But this would be presumed rashly. The founder ought first to be known, that the sect might be known, rather than to draw an inference about the founder from inspection of the sect. But as it is, necessarily being ignorant of the sect because you are ignorant of the founder, or not reviewing the founder because you do not review the sect either, you fasten on the name alone, as if in it you held fast the sect and the founder whom you do not know at all. And yet for philosophers there is open liberty to pass over, in your eyes, to a sect and to carry both the name of its founders and their own; nor does anyone stir up hatred against them, though against your manners, rites, worship, and way of life they openly and publicly bark out all the bitterness of their eloquence, with contempt of the laws, without respect of persons, so that some even hurl their freedom of speech against the emperors themselves with impunity. But the truth, which the age finds most laborious, the philosophers merely aspire to, while the Christians possess it; and therefore those who possess it give more offense, because he who aspires to it makes sport, but he who possesses it defends it. Socrates, in the end, was condemned on that side where he had come closer to the truth, by destroying your gods. Although the Christian name was not yet on earth at that time, still the truth was always condemned. And so you will not deny that he was a wise man, to whom your own Pythian god bore witness. "Of all men," he said, "Socrates is the wisest." The truth conquered Apollo, so that he pronounced sentence against himself; for he confessed that he was not a god, while affirming that the wisest man was the one who denied the gods. But with you he is the less wise for denying the gods, though wise on this very ground, that he denied the gods. In the same way you usually say of us: "A good man, Lucius Titius — only that he is a Christian." And another: "I am astonished that Gaius Seius, a serious man, has become a Christian." With the blindness of folly they praise what they know and condemn what they do not know, and they spoil the thing they know by the thing they do not know. It occurs to no one that perhaps a man is good and prudent for the very reason that he is a Christian, or a Christian for the very reason that he is prudent and good — though it would be more humane to judge the hidden by the manifest than to prejudge the manifest from the hidden. Some, whom before this name they knew as wandering, worthless, dishonest, marvel that they are suddenly reformed, and yet they know better how to marvel than how to follow. Others strive with such obstinacy that they fight even against their own interests, which they could otherwise gain from dealings with this name. I know a husband or two, once anxious about his wife's character — who could not endure even the mice creeping into his bedroom without a groan of suspicion — who, when he learned the cause of her new diligence and unaccustomed captivity, offered his wife all forbearance, declared he was no longer jealous, and would sooner have a harlot for a wife than a Christian. He was free to change his own nature for the worse, but would not permit the woman to be reformed for the better. A father disinherited the son with whom he had ceased to find fault. A master sent to the workhouse the slave he had otherwise found indispensable. As soon as anyone is recognized as a Christian, he is preferred guilty. For the discipline itself is exposed by its own quality, and we are betrayed by nothing other than our own good — just as the wicked shine forth by their own evil. Or are we alone, against the institutions of nature, branded the worst on account of good? For what do we hold out as our mark, except first wisdom, by which we do not adore the trifling works of the human hand; abstinence, by which we keep from what is another's; chastity, which we do not defile even with the eyes; mercy, by which we are bent toward the needy; truth itself, by which we give offense; freedom itself, for which we know how to die? Whoever wishes to understand who the Christians are must of necessity use these tokens.

Some say that the gods were so named for this reason, that "theein" and "seisthai" — the interpretation is to run forward and to be moved. Therefore now this word is not the mark of any majesty; for it is formed from running and motion, not from the dominion of divinity over them. But since even that one God whom we worship is surnamed "theos," and yet neither any motion nor any running of his appears, because he is not even visible to anyone, it is plain that this word is taken from elsewhere, and is proper, because native to itself, an invention of divinity. And so, setting aside the subtlety of that interpretation, it is more likely that the gods were called "theoi" not from running and motion, but borrowed from the appellation of the true God, so that those whom you had likewise fashioned as gods you might surname "theoi." Finally, that it is so, proof is at hand, since you commonly call even all your gods, in whom no office of running or motion is marked, "theoi." And so, if they are equally "theoi," equally immobile, one departs alike from the interpretation of the word and from the opinion of divinity, which, modulated from running and motion, is cut away. But if that name is proper to divinity, and simple, and not interpretative, in that God — reproved in the rest whom you would have to be gods — show also that there is a partnership of quality among them, so that a college may rightly stand by the community of the name through community of substance. Moreover, that "theos" already, by this alone, that he is not in plain sight, is exempt from comparison with those things which are in plain sight, and to the eye and to the sense — but to the sense enough — which is the announcement of testimony to the diversity of the hidden and the manifest. If the elements are openly set before all, if on the contrary God is so before no one, how can you, from that part which you have not seen, engage with what you see? Since, then, you cannot join them by sense or by reason, why do you join them by a word, so as to join them also by power? For behold, Zeno too separates the world's matter from God, or says that he passed through it as honey through the combs. And so matter and God are two words, two things. By the distinction of words even the things are separated; even the condition of matter follows the word. But if it is not matter — because thus too the appellation prescribes — how will those things that are in matter, that is, the elements, be held gods, when members cannot be of an alien kind from the body? But why do I bother with physiological argumentations? The mind ought to have ascended upward from the state of the world, not to descend into uncertainties. The world's form is round, says Plato. That it is square and angular, devised by others, they have gathered, I believe, with a round compass — a thing that labors to be believed alone without a head. But Epicurus, who had said, "What is above us is nothing to us," when he too desired to inspect the heaven, found the sun's orb a foot wide. Frugality, of course, was as yet practiced even in the heavens. Finally, as ambition advanced, the sun too extended its disk; so the Peripatetics marked out that orb as larger. I ask you, what does the lust of conjectures relish? What does the idleness of an affected fastidiousness prove with so great a presumption of asseveration, adorned by the artifice of eloquence? Rightly, then, did Thales of Miletus, while he examines the whole heaven and walks about with his eyes, fall basely into a well, much laughed at by that Egyptian: "On the earth," he said, "you perceived nothing, and you reckon you must scrutinize the heaven?" And so his fall, by way of figure, marks the philosophers — those, namely, who exercise their stupid curiosity upon the things of nature, rather than first upon their artificer and president, destined to have their study vain to themselves.

As for what you say — that the worst and most disgraceful are stained with avarice, luxury, dishonesty — we shall not deny that some are. It is enough even for this to be a testimony to our name, if not all, if not the greater part. It is inevitable that in a body, however whole or pure you would have it, some mole should sprout, or a little wart rise up, or a freckle make a blemish. The very sky, no serenity strains and purifies so far that it is not unsealed by the wisp of some little cloud. A slight stain on the forehead, seen in some one part, while the whole is clean as a sample of it. The greater portion of good uses its slight evil as a testimony to itself. Yet when you prove some of ours to be wicked, by that very fact you prove them to be no Christians. Seek out a sect to which their wickedness may be charged. You yourselves, in conversation, when at any point against us, say, "Why is that man a cheat, if Christians are abstinent? Why is he cruel, if they are merciful?" By this very thing you bear witness that such men are not Christians, when you turn back upon us the question why those called Christians should be such. There is a great distance between the crime and the name, between opinion and truth. For names too have been so established that they have their boundaries between being called and being. How many, in short, are called philosophers, and yet do not fulfill the law of philosophy? All wear the name from their professions, but they bear the name without the excellence of the profession who, by the mere surface of the word, defame the truth. They are not at once what they are called, but because they are not so, they are called so in vain, and they deceive those who attach the reality to the name, when the standing of the name depends upon the reality. And yet such men neither gather nor share with us, having become yours once more through their offenses — since we do not mingle even with those whom your violence and savagery have driven to denial. For surely deserters of the discipline could more easily be kept among us against their will than of their own choice. But for the rest, without cause you call those Christians whom the Christians themselves deny — those who do not know how to deny themselves.

Why, then, are we not converted to some somewhat more human opinion, which may seem deduced from the common sense of all and from simple conjecture? For Varro too mentions it, saying that, besides, the divinity of the elements has been believed, because nothing at all can be born, nourished, or advanced toward the sowing of human life and of the earth without their suffrage; since not even bodies or souls could have sufficed without the tempering of the elements, by which this dwelling of the world, federated by the conditions of the circles, is provided — except that the excess of cold or heat denied human habitation, and therefore the sun is believed a god, which heaps up of its own to the day, ripens the crops with its heat, keeps the year by its stations; the moon, solace of the nights, patroness of the months by its governance; likewise the stars, certain seals of the seasons for marking the times of tillage; finally the heaven itself, under which are all things, the earth, over which are all things, and whatever of these conspires among itself to human advantages. And not only by benefits does the trust of divinity befit the elements, but also from the diverse things which are wont to befall as if from their anger and offense, like thunderbolts, like hail, like burnings, like pestilent breezes, likewise floods, likewise gapings and quakings of the earth; and that they are rightly believed gods, whose nature is to be honored in prosperity, to be feared in adversity, being mistresses, of course, of helping and harming. Moreover, if they are so perceived in the dealings of citizens, they do not likewise render thanks or direct complaints to the very things by which they are helped or harmed, but to those under whose force and power the working of things runs its course. For in pleasures too you do not adjudge the crown for a prize to the pipe or the lyre, but to the artist who tempers pipe and lyre by the force of sweetness. Likewise, when anyone is ill in health, you remember thanks not to the wools nor to the antidotes or the poultices themselves, but to the physicians, by whose work and prudence the remedies come forth. Likewise in adversities, those who are wounded by the sword do not accuse the sword itself or the spear, but the enemy or the robber; and those whom roofs crush do not arraign the tiles or the gutter-tiles, but the age of the building; just as the shipwrecked impute it not to the rock and the waves, but to the storm. Rightly. For it is certain that whatever is done is to be ascribed not to that through which it is done, but to that by which it is done, since he is the head of the deed who appoints both that it be done and by what means it be done — and there are in all things these three titles: what it is, through what it is, and from what it is — because he is prior who wills something to be done, and by what it may be brought about. And so rightly in other matters you act, considering the author; but in physical matters, against nature, your rule by which in other matters you judge wisdom, taking away the highest grade of the author, and considering what is done, not from what it is done. Thus it happens that the powers and judgments of the elements are believed to be what are really their servitudes and offices. In this investigation do we not show, within, the art of some artificer and master of the servitude of the elements, from certain of their works which you do, as a power? But the gods do not serve; therefore those things which serve are not gods. Or let them teach that it commonly happens, so that from the license of passivity liberty may be approved, from liberty dominion, from dominion divinity be understood. For if all these things over us are constituted in fixed courses, lawful runnings, proper spaces, equal turns, after the manner of a law, and remember to meet for the rolling of the seasons and the exercising of the seasons' guidances — do they not, from the very observance of their conditions, and the fidelity of their works, and the persistence of their courses, and the care of their changes, the memory of their reciprocations, persuade you that some dominion presides over them, to which all the world's business may seem to appear, reaching to the advantage and injury of the human race? For you cannot say that they do these things for themselves and care for themselves, nor dispose anything for the sake of men, since for this very reason you defend a divinity in the elements, because you feel yourself either helped or harmed by them. For if they provide for themselves, you owe them nothing.

To these our propositions and answers, which the truth furnishes from its own resources, as often as your conscience is squeezed and confined — the silent witness of its own ignorance — you flee for refuge, in your distress, to a certain little altar, that is, the authority of the laws: that surely they would not punish this sect unless its demerits had been established before the framers of the laws. What then has prevented the same thing from being established before the executors of the laws as well, since in the case of other crimes, which are likewise barred and punished by the laws, the penalty is held back unless inquiry is first made? For instance, a murderer, an adulterer, are bound by the law: yet the manner of the deed is examined, and even so the kind of act is known to all. The laws punish the Christian. If there is any deed of a Christian, it ought to be brought to light. No law forbids inquiry; rather, inquiry serves the laws. For how will you observe a law by avoiding what the law forbids, when the diligence of avoidance is taken away through the failure to recognize what you should observe? No law owes the awareness of its own justice to itself, but to those from whom it claims obedience. Otherwise a law is suspect if it is unwilling to prove itself. Rightly, then, so long as it is not known what they persecute, the laws against the Christians are deemed just and to be revered and observed; rightly, after recognition, found most unjust, they are spat upon together with their swords and gibbets and lions. The honor of an unjust law is nothing. But, as I suppose, the injustice of certain laws is not even in doubt, since every day you temper their harshness and their wickedness by new decrees and ordinances.

Come now, do you grant that divinity ought not only not to run after the manner of a slave, but above all to stand entire, and ought neither to be diminished nor intercepted nor corrupted? For all its felicity is gone, if it ever suffers anything. But behold, the stars too perish, and attest that they have perished. The moon too confesses how much it has lost, when it recovers it. Indeed you are accustomed to consider its greater losses in the mirror of water, so that I would no longer believe in any part what the magi know. The sun itself too has often been assailed by eclipse. Feign whatever reasons you like for the misfortunes of the heavenly bodies; God will not wish either to be made less or to cease to be. Let the patronages of human doctrine, then, look to themselves, which by the artifice of conjecture counterfeit wisdom and truth. For at other times nature is such that he who has spoken the better seems to have spoken the more truly, not he who has spoken the more truly, the better. But for him to whom the matter is examined, surely he will speak the more plausibly who says that these elements are ruled by someone rather than that they move of their own accord; therefore they are not gods which are under someone. But if there is error in this, it is better to err simply than, like the physicists, diligently. Indeed, if you look to the mythical, mortality already errs better in the physical by ascribing divinity to those things which it thinks are perceived above man by position and force and magnitude and divinity. For what is above man, you may believe near to God.

Whence, then, you ask, has so much report against us been licensed — report whose testimony may perhaps have sufficed for the framers of the laws? Who, I pray, was the surety to them then, or thereafter to you, of its trustworthiness? Report it is. Is this not she: "Report, an evil than which nothing else is swifter"? Why an evil, if she were always true? Not by falsehood — and even then least of all, when she carries true things, does she cease from her lust for lying, so as not to weave the false into the true, adding, subtracting, confounding by variety. What of this? That such is her condition, that she persists only as long as she lies. For she lives just so long as she proves nothing; since once approved she falls, and as if discharged from the office of reporting she departs. Thereafter the matter is held as fact, the matter is named as fact, and no one says, for instance, "They say this was done at Rome," or "Report has it that he drew that province by lot," but "He drew the province," and "This was done at Rome." No one names Report except one who is unsure, since no one is made certain by report but by knowledge; no one believes Report except a fool, since the wise man does not believe the uncertain. Report, with however great ambition she has been spread abroad, must at some time have arisen from a single mouth; thence she creeps, as it were, through the relays of tongues and ears, and the slight flaw in her origins darkens the rumor, so that no one reflects whether that first mouth sowed lies — which often happens, either through the spirit of rivalry, or at the bidding of suspicion, or even from the fresh pleasure of lying. But it is well that time reveals all things, as your own maxims and proverbs bear witness, and nature itself, which is so ordered that nothing lies hidden, even what report has not betrayed. See, then, what a portent you have suborned against us, since what report once brought forth, and over so long a time has fortified into belief, it has been unable to prove even to this day. Under the emperor Augustus this name arose; under Tiberius its discipline shone out; under Nero its condemnation gained strength — so that from this very fact you may weigh the person of the persecutor. If that emperor was pious, then Christians are impious; if just, if chaste, then Christians are unjust and incestuous; if not a public enemy, then we are public enemies. What we are, the condemner himself made plain, punishing surely what was a rival to himself. And yet, when all his other measures were erased, this Neronian institution alone remained — just, in short, as being unlike its author. So our age numbers not yet two hundred and fifty years. So many wicked deeds in the meantime, so many crosses attaining divinity, so many infants slaughtered, so many loaves stained with blood, so many extinguishings of lamps, so many wanderings of unions — and still for the Christians report alone decides. It has indeed a grand foundation in the fault of the human character: more readily does it lie in bitter and atrocious matters. For the more prone you are to malice, the more apt to believe an evil; in short, a false evil is more readily believed than a true good. Yet if injustice had left any room among you for prudence, justice surely demanded, for testing the trustworthiness of report, that you look closely to see by whom report could have been given to the crowd, and so to the whole world. From the Christians themselves I do not suppose it, since by the very form and law of all mysteries silence is the trust that is owed. How much more in the case of such things as, even if betrayed, would not in the meantime escape the present punishment of the consequence? If, then, they are not their own betrayers, it follows that outsiders are. I ask you, whence comes the knowledge to outsiders, when even lawful and licit mysteries guard against every outside witness, unless the unlawful ones spurn this less? Yet for outsiders, both to be ignorant and to invent is more in keeping. The curiosity of household members has stolen its way through crannies and caverns. What then? Will your household members betray these things to you? In every case we are betrayed by none more than by these — how much more so, if the atrocity be so great that the justice of indignation breaks every bond of household trust? The mind could not contain what it shuddered at, the eye what it dreaded. This too is a wonder, if both he who, by so great a right of impatience, leapt forward to inform did not also long to prove, and he who heard did not take care also to see — since the reward is equal both for the informer, if he proves what he has reported, and for the hearer, if he believes for himself what he hears. "Then," you say, "it was first reported and exhibited, heard and inspected, and thereafter committed to report." This indeed surpasses all wonder, if a thing was caught but once that is always being committed — unless we have by now ceased to do such things. Yet we are still called by the same name, and counted among the same charges, and we grow in number by the day; the more we are, the more we are hated by the many. The hatred grows the more as its subject-matter grows: with the multitude of the accused increasing, why does the multitude of informers not increase in like measure? So far as I know, our manner of life has become better known; you know the days of our assemblies, and so we are both besieged and crushed and detained in our very secret congregations. Yet who has ever come upon a half-eaten corpse? Who has detected the marks of teeth in a bloodstained loaf? Who, when the darkness was burst by a sudden light, has recognized any foul — not to say incestuous — tokens? If by a bribe we obtain not to be dragged out into public as such, why are we crushed at all? We could also escape being dragged out altogether. For who either sells or buys back the betrayal of any crime without the crime itself? But why should I shrink from outside spies and informers, since you bring forward such charges as are not published by us ourselves with the loudest outcry — either at once when heard, if they are shown beforehand, or later when discovered, if for a time they are concealed? For without doubt it is the custom for those wishing to be initiated to go first to the master of the rites or the father. Then he will say: "You need an infant, still a little child, to be slain, and a quantity of bread to be soaked in the blood; besides, lamp-stands, which dogs tied to them may overturn, and morsels to entice the same dogs; but a mother also or a sister is needful to you." What if there are none? I suppose you cannot be a lawful Christian. These things, I ask you, do they bear to be betrayed by others when proclaimed beforehand? It is a different matter for them to know. First the business of deception is carried through: to the unwitting both feast and union are presented; for they had never before heard anything of Christian mysteries. Yet afterwards they must of necessity come to know, since the rites must be ministered to others whom they themselves bring in. But for the rest, how empty it is that the uninitiated should know what the priest does not! They keep silence, then, and accept it, and break out in no Thyestean or Oedipal tragedy, and do not drag it forth before the people. Trust takes from its ministers and masters, and from those by now instructed, no more biting reproach. If nothing of the kind is proved, we must reckon it to be some great thing or other, the recompense of which consists in the endurance of such atrocities. O wretched and pitiable nations, behold, we set before you the pledge of our discipline. It promises eternal life to its followers and keepers; on the contrary, to the profane and the hostile it threatens eternal punishment by eternal fire; for both causes the resurrection of the dead is proclaimed. We shall see about the credit of these things, when they are set out in their place; meanwhile believe, as we do. For I wish to know, if you are ready to approach by such crimes, whether you do so as we do. Come, whoever you are, plunge the iron into the infant; or if it is another's office, then merely look on at the soul dying before it has lived; at least catch the fresh blood, in which you may soak your bread, and eat freely; meanwhile recline, count the places where mother or sister has pressed the couch; mark carefully, so that, when the darkness has rushed in — testing, of course, the diligence of each — you may not stray by attacking a stranger: you will have committed a sacrilege, unless it be incest. When you have accomplished these things, you will live forever. I would have you answer, if you value eternity so highly? No — for that very reason you do not believe; and even if you should believe, I deny that you would be willing; and even if you were willing, I deny that you would be able. But why should others be able, if you cannot? Why should you not be able, if others can? At what price do you wish impunity, eternity, to be bought? Or do these seem to us to be worth buying by any means at all? Are the rows of teeth different in Christians, and the caverns of their throats, and their sinews for the lust of incest? I do not think so. For it is enough for us to be distinguished from your position by truth alone.

But, to pass over to the mythical, which is allotted to the poets, I do not know whether it is worth seeking the equal of our mediocrity, whether they are confirmed by such documents of divinity, as Mopsus the African and Amphiaraus the Boeotian. For this species is now to be touched on lightly, of which the account will be rendered in its place. Meanwhile that these at least were men is plain even from this, that you do not consistently call them gods, but heroes. Why, then, do we contend? If divinity was to be assigned to the dead, surely not to such as these. Behold, you, with the same license of presumption, defame the heaven with the tombs of your kings; do you not — those proved by justice, virtue, piety, and every such good — honor with the solace of such consecration, content for such men to be even derided as you perjure yourselves; while on the contrary you take away even their former rewards of human glory from the impious, the base, you tear up their decrees and titles, you drag down their images, you restrike the coinage? But that surveyor of all things, the approver — nay, the bestower — of good things, will he prostitute to the crowd the ordination of so great a generosity of his, and will more diligence and justice be permitted to men in distributing divinities? Will the courtiers of kings and princes be cleaner than the supreme God? And yet you shudder at and turn away from vagabonds, exiles, the poor, the weak, the basely born, the dishonorably trained; against the incestuous, adulterers, ravishers, even parricides, you adorn yourselves with laws. Is it to be laughed at or to be raged at, that such gods are believed as men ought not to be? But indeed in this mythical kind, which the poets report, with what uncertainty do you act around the modesty of conscience and the defense of modesty! For as often as we reproach the wretched or base or atrocious deeds of the gods, you defend them as fabulous, by the plea of poetic license; as often as silence is kept of its own accord about such poetic matter, not only do you not shudder, but you even honor it, and hold it among the necessary arts, and finally, through this initiating literature, you advance the studies of free birth. The poets, accusers of the gods, Plato decreed should be banished; Homer himself, crowned indeed, should be driven from the city. But since you receive them and retain them, why should you not believe them as they recount such things of your gods? Therefore, if you believe the poets, why do you worship such gods? If you worship them for this reason, that you do not believe the poets, why do you bestow praise on liars, and do not beware lest you offend those whose detractors you honor? To be sure, faith is not to be exacted of the poets. Do you not, who say the gods were made after death, confess them men before death? What then is new, if those who were men are polluted by human chances or crimes or fables? You do not believe the poets, when from their relations you have even arranged certain sacred rites. Why is the priest of Ceres carried off, if Ceres did not suffer such a thing? Why are others' children sacrificed to Saturn, if he spared his own? Why is the male of the Idaean goddess amputated, if no youth, too disdainful, was castrated by her in the grief of frustrated lust? Why do the Lanuvian women not taste of the Herculean banquet, if it was not on women's account that it was begun? The poets lie, to be sure! But not for this reason — that your gods did such things, when they were men, nor that they ascribed divine foulnesses to divinity — when meanwhile it has seemed to you more credible that they were gods, but not such, than that they were such, but not gods.

Plainly, we are called a third race. Are we some dog-headed creatures, or Shadow-foots? Or some Antipodes from the underworld? If there is among you any reasoning at all in this, I would have you produce the first and second race, that the third may thereby be established. Psammetichus, indeed, thought he had explored the matter of the first-born by his own ingenuity. For he is said to have handed over infants fresh from birth, to be reared apart from human dealings, to a nurse whom for that very purpose he had deprived of her tongue, so that, being wholly exiled from the human voice, they might form their speech not from hearing, but uttering it from themselves, might mark out as the first nation that one whose sound nature had dictated. The first word reported was "bekkos"; its interpretation among the Phrygians is the name for bread; the Phrygians are thenceforth held to be the first race. But this will be the one item among the vanities of your fables not to be reviewed by us idly, since by it we aim to show that your trust is given to vanities rather than to truths. Or is it at all credible that, with such a member cut away, the very organ of the soul laid waste and cut, indeed, to the root, the throat castrated — which even from outside is dangerously wounded — and corruption thence flowing back into the vitals, and at the last food failing for some while, life endured in that nurse? Come now, suppose she did keep her life by the remedies of Philomela — whose silence the more prudent interpret not from any cutting of the tongue, but from the blush of shame. If, then, she lived, she could have stammered out something muffled. And a disjointed sound and ringing without the modulation of the lips, from an open mouth, with the tongue stupefied, can be forced from the throat alone. This perhaps the infants, since it was the only one, more easily contrived a little more melodiously — being themselves of nimble tongue — and hit upon as the discovery of some interpretation. Let the Phrygians be first now; still the Christians are not third. For how many other series of nations after the Phrygians? But reconsider, lest those whom you call a third race should hold the first place, since indeed there is no nation that is not Christian. And so whatever nation is first, it is none the less Christian. With ridiculous madness you call us latest and name us third. But it is by superstition that we are reckoned a third race, not by nation, so that there are Romans, Jews, and then Christians. But where then are the Greeks? Or if they are counted among the superstitions of the Romans, since indeed Rome solicited even the gods of Greece — where at least are the Egyptians, themselves, so far as I know, of a private and curious religion? Moreover, if those who hold the third place are so monstrous, what are we to think of those who go before in the first and second?

There remains that national kind of gods among the peoples, whom private knowledge teaches were taken up by caprice, not for the knowledge of truth. I think God, therefore, is everywhere known, everywhere present, everywhere ruling, to be worshipped by all, to be won over by all. But indeed, since even those whom the whole world worships in common fall short of the proof of true divinity, how much more these whom not even their own townsmen know? For what fit authority has gone before such a theology, which even report has deserted? How many are there who know, by sight or hearing, Atargatis of the Syrians, Caelestis of the Africans, Varsutina of the Moors, Obodas and Dusares of the Arabs, Belenus of Noricum, or those whom Varro sets down: Deluentinus of the Casinenses, Visidianus of the Narnienses, Numiternus of the Atinates, Anchararia of the Asculani, and Nortia, whom the Volsinienses have received — gods whose names not even in dignity differ from human surnames? Enough do I laugh too at the decurion gods of each municipality, whose honor is bounded within their own walls. To what lengths this liberty of adopting gods has advanced, the superstitions of the Egyptians teach, who worship even private beasts, cats, crocodiles, and their own serpent. It is a small matter, if they have even consecrated a man — I mean him whom now not Egypt or Greece, but the whole world worships, and by whom the Africans swear; about whose state, what can be conjectured from our literature, so as to seem plausible, has been set down. For that Serapis was once called Joseph, of the race of the holy ones. The youngest among the rest of the brothers, but loftier in genius, sold into Egypt by those same brothers through envy, he served in the household of the king of the Egyptians, Pharaoh. Desired by a queen less chaste, but because he did not comply, on the contrary, accused by her to the king, he is committed to prison. There, having interpreted certain dreams not amiss, he showed the force of his spirit. Meanwhile the king too dreams certain terrible things. Drawn forth — for he had been summoned — Joseph was able to expound; he gave proofs out of prison, he opens the dream to the king: that those seven fattest, overflowing oxen signify as many years of plenty; the latter, equally seven, lean, foretell the want of the following seven years. And so he advises about storing up defenses against a future famine from the former plenty. The king believed; the outcome of events proved him both prudent and holy ever and necessary. And so Pharaoh set him over all Egypt, both to be provisioned and thereafter to be cared for. This man they called Serapis from the head-dress with which his head was adorned; whose head-dress, of a modius's shape, seals the memory of his provisioning, and that the care of the crops was upon his head, it appears from the very ears of corn by which it is marked round about. For this reason too they dedicated the dog, which they reckon among the powers below, under his right hand, because under his hand the care of the Egyptians was compressed. And they add Pharia, whom the derivation of the name shows to be the daughter of king Pharaoh. For then too Pharaoh, among the rest of his honors and rewards, had given his daughter also to him in marriage. But because they had undertaken to worship both beasts and men, they combined both faces into one Anubis, in whom that quarrelsome race might be seen rather to have consecrated the proofs of its own nature and condition — recoiling against its own kings, cast down among strangers, and indeed itself a slave even in gluttony and canine filthiness.

But why should I marvel at your vanities, when by a natural cast malice and folly have grown together, embodied as one, under the same proprietor of error? Truly, since I do not marvel, I must enumerate, so that you, recognizing yourselves, may marvel into what depth of folly you fall — you who would have us be the cause of every public disaster or injury. If the Tiber has overflowed, if the Nile has not overflowed, if the sky has stood still, if the earth has quaked, if famine has wasted, if pestilence has afflicted — at once the cry of all: "The Christians to the lion!" As if those who fear the true God had any small thing, or anything else, to fear. I suppose it is as despisers of your gods that we provoke these darts of theirs. As we have said above, our age numbers not yet three hundred years; how many disasters, before that span, fell upon the whole world, upon single cities and provinces? How many wars, foreign and civil? How many plagues, famines, fires, gapings and quakings of the earth, has the age recorded? Where then were the Christians, when the Roman state supplied so many histories of its labors? Where then were the Christians, when the islands of Hiera, Anaphe and Delos and Rhodos and Cea went to the bottom with many thousands of men — or that one, greater than Asia or Africa, which Plato records as sunk in the Atlantic sea? When fire poured from heaven upon Volsinii, and upon Pompeii from its own mountain? When by an earthquake the Corinthian sea was snatched away? When a cataclysm abolished the whole world? Where then were — I will not say the Christians, despisers of the gods — but your very gods, whom places, towns, prove to be later than that disaster, in which they were born, lived, were buried, even those they founded? For otherwise they would not have survived to the present, except as offspring later than that disaster. If you do not care to read again and unroll the testimonies of the ages, otherwise reported to you, then, above all, that you may not pronounce your gods most unjust, who on account of despisers harm even their own worshippers, do you not then prove that you yourselves are in error, if you hand down gods who do not distinguish you from the deserts of the profane? But if, as one or another most empty fellow says, they are angry with you also for this reason, that you are negligent about our extermination, then the matter is settled concerning their weakness and mediocrity: for they would not be angry with you for slackening in their vengeance, if they could do anything of themselves. Although you confess this on other occasions too, as often as you seem to avenge them by our punishment. If one thing is defended by another, it is defended by a greater. Let the gods then be ashamed to be defended by man.

These things, according to the threefold disposition of Varro's divinity, we have set out, the more notable or more signal of them, so that it may now seem enough to have answered concerning the physical kind, the poetical, the national. But since all the substitution is now not of the philosophers nor of the poets nor of the peoples, by whom it was handed down, but of the dominant Romans, by whom it was seized, by whom it built up authority for itself, another breadth of human error must now be entered by us — nay, a forest is to be cut down, which on every side, from the conceived seeds of superstitions, has overshadowed the boyhood of vice. But the Romans' gods too Varro disposed three ways: into certain, uncertain, and select. So great a vanity! For what had they to do with the uncertain, if they had the certain? Unless perhaps they wished to take up the Attic stupor. For at Athens too there is an altar inscribed: "TO THE UNKNOWN GODS." Does anyone, then, worship what he does not know? Then if they had the certain, they ought to have been content, and not to desire the select. In which they are caught out as irreligious too. For if gods are picked out like onions, those not picked out are pronounced bad. But we recognize the Romans' gods two ways, common and proper — that is, those they have with all, and those they themselves have devised. And are not these called public and adventitious? For this the altars teach: of the adventitious at the shrine of Carna, of the public on the Palatine. Wherefore, since the common gods are comprehended both in the physical and in the mythical, it is now done with these. It now pleases to speak of the species of proper ones. Let us be amazed at that third kind of Roman gods, the hostile gods, because no other nation has found out so much superstition for itself. The rest we arrange into two species: some taken up from men, others conceived in another manner. Therefore, since the same coloring of the consecration of the dead serves them, as if on account of life's merits, we must of necessity oppose the same answer also: that no one of these either was worth so much. They believed Aeneas a loving father — a soldier never glorious, disabled by a stone. What a weapon, how common and currish, so much the more ignoble the wound! But Aeneas too is found a traitor to his country, as much Aeneas as Antenor. And if they will not have this true, Aeneas certainly, his country in flames, deserted his comrades, to be subjected to the Punic woman, who did not, in Aeneas's cowardly fashion, accompany her husband Hasdrubal as he gently supplicated the enemy, snatching her children with her — she has it in her to have a fatherland and a father not by knowing how to flee, but she fell upon the fires of burning Carthage as into the embrace of her perishing fatherland. Pious Aeneas, on account of a single boy and a decrepit old man, while Priam and Astyanax were left forsaken? Yet the more to be detested by the Romans, who, for the safety of their princes and their house, swear against their children and wives and all their pledges. They consecrate the son of Venus, and this Vulcan suffers knowingly and Juno allows. If sons sit in heaven through the piety of their parents, why are not rather those Argive youths held gods, who, lest their mother should commit a sin in the rites, drew her yoke in more than human fashion? Why not rather she a goddess, who was the more pious, that daughter who reared her father, failing from hunger in prison, with her own breasts? What else of Aeneas was glorious, except that in the Laurentine battle he nowhere appeared? Perhaps again, in his wonted manner, he fled the battle as a deserter. Romulus likewise is a god after death. If because he founded a city? Why not others, even to women, founders of cities? To be sure, Romulus both killed his brother and ravished by guile the maidens of others. Therefore is he a god, therefore Quirinus, because then his parents were called upon for help through him. What did Sterculus deserve toward divinity? If he was diligent in helping the fields with dung, Augeas contributed more dung. If Faunus, son of Picus, was hauled into court, struck in his mind, he ought rather to have been cured than consecrated. If Faunus's daughter excelled in chastity, so that she did not even consort among men, either from barbarity or from awareness of deformity or from shame at her father's madness, how much worthier a Good Goddess Penelope, who, dwelling among so many most worthless suitors, protected her besieged chastity and kept it! There is also Sanctus, who obtained a shrine from king Plotius on account of his hospitality; Ulysses too could have conferred on you one more god from the most humane Alcinous.

Pour out now all your poisons, drive in all the darts of calumny against this name; I shall not cease henceforth to repel them, though afterwards they will be blunted by the exposition of our whole discipline. But now I shall turn these very same charges, plucked from our body, back upon you; I shall show the same wounds of crimes buried in you, so that you may fall by your own swords and arguments. First, then, as to what you direct against us in your general accusation — a divorce from the institutions of our forefathers — consider again and again whether you do not share this crime with us. For behold, throughout all the conduct of life and discipline, I recognize in you antiquity corrupted, indeed destroyed. Of the laws, indeed, it has already been said above, that you have buried them under new decrees and ordinances day by day. But as for the rest of the ordering of human conduct, it plainly lies open how much you have changed from your forefathers — in dress, in bearing, in equipment, in your very food, in your very speech; for you banish the old as rancid. Antiquity is everywhere shut out, in business, in offices; your authority has cast down all the authority of the forefathers. To be sure — and this is the more to your reproach — you always praise the old things, and none the less reject them. By what perverseness ought so many vanities of the forefathers to remain among you, to be approved, when you reject the very things you approve? But even the very thing you seem to keep and defend most faithfully as handed down from the forefathers — the very ground on which you most demand us guilty of transgression, on which the whole hatred of the Christian name is roused — I mean the worship of the gods — I shall show to be likewise destroyed and despised by you. Except that there is no reason why we should be held despisers of the gods either, since no one despises what he knows to be wholly nonexistent. That which exists at all can be despised; that which is nothing suffers nothing. Therefore, by those for whom they exist, they must of necessity suffer. By so much the more are you burdened, believing them to exist and despising them, worshipping and spitting upon them, honoring and provoking them. One may recognize this, above all, even from this: that since you worship some gods and others worship others, those whom you do not worship you of course despise. The preference of one cannot be without insult to another, nor is any choice made up without rejection. He who, out of many, takes up one, has scorned the one he does not take up. But so many and so great cannot be worshipped by all. Then already, at the first, you despised them, not fearing, of course, so to establish them that they could not all be worshipped. But indeed those most wise and most prudent forefathers, whose institutions you do not know how to renounce, especially in the person of your gods, are themselves caught out as impious. I lie, if they had not at some time decreed that no commander should dedicate a shrine he had vowed in war before the senate had approved it — as happened to Marcus Aemilius, who had vowed it to the god Alburnus. For surely it was a most impious — nay, most contemptuous — thing to commit, to place the honor of divinity in the arbitration and caprice of a human verdict, so that a god might not exist except for him whom the senate had permitted to exist. Often the censors, without consulting the people, leveled shrines to the ground. Liberty's Father himself, with his rites, the consuls, by the senate's authority, banished not only from the city but from all Italy. Moreover, Varro records that Serapis and Isis and Harpocrates and Anubis were forbidden the Capitol, and that their altars, cast down by the senate, were restored only by the violence of the populace. Yet even Gabinius the consul, on the Kalends of January, when he could scarcely approve the victims because of the crowd of the populace, since he had decreed nothing concerning Serapis and Isis, held the senate's censure of more weight than the impulse of the crowd, and forbade altars to be set up. You have, then, in your forefathers — if not the name, yet the sect — a Christian sect, one that neglects the gods. Of these, if you at least were unimpaired in your honors, you would be guilty of injured religion; but I find that from you proceeded an advance both of superstition and of impiety alike. For how much the more irreligious are you found! Your private gods, whom you call Lares and Penates by household consecration, you trample by household license, selling and pawning them according to need and will. Indeed, the sacrileges of such contumacy would be more tolerable, except that they are by now the more contemptuous for being trifling. But the complaints of private and household gods are aided by some consolation, that you treat the public gods more basely and more contumeliously. First of all, those whom you have entered on the auction-list, you have made subject to the tax-farmers; every five years you assign them, proscribed among your revenues. Thus the Serapeum, thus the Capitol, is sought, knocked down, leased, like the forum, under the same voice of the auctioneer, the same levy of the quaestor. But fields laden with tribute are cheaper, men's heads taxed with a poll-tax are baser — for these are the marks and penalties of captivity — yet the gods, the more they are tributary, the more holy; nay, the more holy, the more tributary. Majesty is set up for profit, the dealing is proscribed by religion, holiness goes begging for a lease. You exact a fee for the temple's site, for entrance to the sacred place, for the offerings, for the victims. You sell the whole of divinity. It is not lawful for it to be worshipped free. In short, more is paid over to the tax-farmers than to the priests. Nor did the contumely of taxed gods suffice — a contumely to be reckoned, of course, from contempt — nor are you content not to have honored the gods, but you also cheapen whatever god you have by some indignity. For what do you do at all to honor them that you do not equally render to your dead? You build temples to the gods, and equally temples to the dead; you build altars to the gods, and equally altars to the dead; you write the same inscriptions upon them, you give the same forms to the statues, according to each one's art or trade or age: an old man is figured from Saturn, a beardless youth from Apollo, a maiden from Diana, and the soldier is consecrated in Mars, and the smith in Vulcan. Nothing then is to be wondered at, if you slay the same victims to the dead as to the gods, and burn the same incense. Who could excuse that contumely, which reckons the dead, however it may, together with the gods? To kings, indeed, even priesthoods and sacred apparatus are ascribed, and chariots and cars and couches spread for sun and feast, festivities and games. Plainly, since heaven lies open to them — this too not without contumely to the gods: first, because it was unbecoming that others should be numbered with them, if it be granted to become gods after death; secondly, because the witness of a man received into heaven would not so freely and openly perjure himself before the people, did he not despise those by whom he swears, both himself and those who allow him to perjure himself. For they themselves agree that what they swear by is nothing — nay, more, they even reward the man, because he has publicly despised the avengers of perjury. Although, among you, how few are pure of perjury? Indeed, by now the danger of swearing by the gods has vanished, the greater religion being held of swearing by Caesar — which itself too belongs to the obscuring of your gods; for those who perjure themselves by Caesar would more readily be punished than those who do so by any Jupiter. But contempt is more honorable, having a certain glory of pride; for it comes sometimes even from confidence, either of conscience's security or of the mind's natural loftiness. But derision, the more wanton it is, the more marked is its bite of contumely. Recognize then how you are found to be deriders of your own deities. I do not speak of what you are in sacrificing — that you slaughter whatever is sickly and wasting, but of the fat and whole offer up the superfluous bits not fit to eat, the heads and hooves, the pluckings of feathers and bristles, and whatever you would have thrown away at home anyway. I pass over what will seem matters of the common crowd or of sacrilegious gluttony, nearly suited to the religion of the forefathers. But the most learned, the gravest — so far as gravity and prudence are believed to profit from learning — are always also the most irreverent toward your gods; nor does their literature cease to bring forward what is the more shamefully vain or false about the gods. Let me begin from your own study, that of him from whom every more wicked one dreams, to whom you adjudge as much honor as you have detracted from your gods, magnifying the man who made sport of them. We still remember Homer. He, I suppose, is the one who treated the divine majesty after the human condition, steeping the gods in human chances and passions; who, of the gods set at variance by favoritism, composed, as it were, gladiatorial matches: he wounds Venus with a human arrow, holds Mars thirteen months in chains, perhaps to perish; the same poet shows Jupiter almost suffering the like from the commons of heaven, or wrings tears from him over Sarpedon, or brings him in luxuriating most foully with Juno, with the desire of his lust commended by the commemoration and enumeration of his mistresses. Thereafter, what poet, on the authority of his prince, was not insolent toward the gods, either by betraying the true or by feigning the false? And did the tragic or comic poets spare to prelude with the toils and penalties of a god? I say nothing of the philosophers, whom pride of severity and hardness of discipline, secure from all fear, and even some breath of truth, rouse up against the gods. In short, Socrates too, to their contumely, swears by an oak, a dog, and a goat. For although for this reason he was condemned, when the Athenians repented of the condemnation, so that they even punished his accusers, the testimony is restored to Socrates, and I can turn it back, that there was approved in him what is now reproved in us. But Diogenes too made some sport, I know not what, of Hercules; and the Roman Diogenes, Varro of the pen, brings in three hundred Joves — or "Jupiters," as we must say — without heads. The other geniuses of wantonness administer even your pleasures through the disgrace of the gods. Look among yourselves at the sacrilegious charms of the Lentuli and the Hostii, whether you laugh at mimes or at your gods in their tricks and jests; but you also receive with great pleasure the writings of actors, which mark out all the foulness of the gods. Majesties are debauched before you in an impure body. A defamed and degraded head puts on the image of any god you please. The Sun mourns his son struck by the thunderbolt, while you rejoice; Cybele sighs for the disdainful shepherd, while you do not blush; and you bear to have the praises of Jupiter set to music. Plainly you are more religious in the gladiators' arena, where, over human blood, over the filth of penalties, your gods likewise dance — plots and histories devised for paying out the guilty, or the guilty are punished in the very persons of the gods. We have often seen Attis, the god from Pessinus, castrated; and one who was burned alive had put on the dress of Hercules. We have laughed, too, at the noonday sport made of the gods, when Father Dis, Jupiter's brother, conducts the obsequies of the gladiators with a mallet; when Mercury, winged on his bald head, fiery in his caduceus, tests with a hot iron the bodies already lifeless, or feigning death. Each of these things, who could go on to investigate, whether they disturb the honor of divinity, whether they level the height of majesty? They are surely to be reckoned matters of contempt, both on the part of those who do such things and on the part of those who so receive them. Wherefore I do not know but that your gods may complain more of you than of us. Despised on the one hand, you flatter them on the other; you buy off whatever you transgress; and finally you are permitted to do as you will to those you have willed into being. But we wholly turn away from them.

I hasten to fouler things. Your authors were not ashamed to make public about Larentina. She was a hireling harlot, whether as the nurse of Romulus — and therefore a she-wolf because a harlot — or as the mistress of Hercules, and of a now dead Hercules, that is, of one now a god.
