For they say that his temple-keeper, alone by chance in the shrine, playing at dice, that he might represent to himself the playmate he did not have, played one hand in the name of Hercules, the other from his own person, with this stake: if he himself won, he should take from Hercules's offerings a little supper and a little harlot; but if Hercules — that is, the other hand — he should furnish the same to Hercules. Hercules's hand won. This too could be ascribed to his twelve titles. The temple-keeper pays out the supper to Hercules, hires the harlot Larentina; the fire that loosed Hercules's own body dines, and the altar consumed all. Larentina sleeps alone in the shrine, and the woman from the pander's school boasts that she served Hercules in her dreams, and might well, while she contemplated him in her mind, suffer it in a dream. As she came forth from the shrine at first dawn, a certain young man, a third Hercules as they say, desired her, invited her to himself. She complies, mindful that this had been told her by Hercules for her advantage, and at any rate obtains that they be joined in lawful wedlock — for it was not permitted with impunity to have to do with a god's harlot — and her spouse writes her also his heir. Soon, near death, she bequeathed to the Roman people a field, ample enough, which she had won through Hercules. Hence she sought divinity for her daughters too, whom the divine Larentina ought to have made heirs as well. The Romans' deities are increased by her dignity. Doubtless she alone of so many wives of Hercules was dear, alone indeed rich, and so far the more fortunate than Ceres, who pleased one dead. By so many examples and names among you, who could not have been affirmed a god? Who, finally, disputed Antinous's title to divinity? More comely was Ganymede, or dearer to his lover? Heaven lies open among you to the dead. You force a road from the lower world to the stars. Everywhere harlots ascend, lest you think you bestow much on your kings.

Nor are we guilty in this name only of having deserted the common religion, but of having brought in over it a monstrous superstition. For, as some of you have dreamed, an ass's head is our god — a suspicion that Cornelius Tacitus raised. For he, in the fourth book of his Histories, where he treats of the Jewish war, beginning from the origin of the nation, and arguing as he pleased both of the origin itself and of the name of the religion, reports that the Jews, on their expedition, laboring in vast places from want of water, escaped by following wild asses, which, after pasture, were reckoned to be seeking water, as guides to a spring; and that thus, for that favor, the likeness of a similar beast came to be worshipped by the Jews. From this, I suppose, it was presumed that we too, as near to the Jewish religion, are initiated to the same image. But indeed the same Cornelius Tacitus — that most talkative of liars — forgetting his own assertion, reports in his later books that Pompey the Great, when the Jews were subdued and Jerusalem taken, entered the temple and, searching it thoroughly, found nothing of an image. Where then would that god have been? Surely nowhere more than in a temple so memorable, especially one closed to all except the priests, where they would not have feared a stranger. But why should I defend the point, having professed meanwhile a temporary confession of all things to be transferred equally to you? Let it be believed that our god is some ass-headed figure; will you at any rate deny that you have the same things along with us? Truly you worship whole asses, with their Epona too, and all draught-beasts and cattle and beasts, which you consecrate alike with their mangers. And perhaps this is what you reproach us with — that, among the worshippers of all creatures, we alone are ass-keepers.

Nor are you content to affirm as gods those who in time past were seen, heard, and handled, whose effigies were described, their dealings recorded, their memory propagated; you demand from heaven I know not what shades, incorporeal, lifeless, and names from things, and you sanction them, dividing the whole state of man among single powers, even from the very conception in the womb: so that there should be a certain god Consevius, who presides over the sowings of intercourse, and Fluviona, who keeps the infant in the womb; hence Vitumnus and Sentinus, through whom the infant lives and first feels; then Diespiter, who leads the boy through to birth. When first they gave birth, there was also Candelifera, since they gave birth by candle-light, and the other goddesses who are named from the offices of birth. They willed the province of Postverta to be the helping of those born wrong, of Prosa-Carmentis of those born right. There is a god named also from speech, Farinus, and others from talking, Locutius. Cunina is at hand for the eye heavy with watching, and supplies rest. There is a rearer, Levana, and likewise Rumina. A wonder, that gods were not provided for washing away the infants' filth. Hence too Potina and Edula, for the first food to be taken and drink to be received, and Statina for setting the infant up. They have Adeona of approaching, Abeona of departing. They have also a Domiduca, and a goddess Mens, who makes the mind good and likewise bad; likewise of the will Volumnus and Voleta. They have also Paventina of dread, Venilia of hope, Volupia of pleasure, Praestitia of excellence; likewise from action Peragenor, from counsels Consus, Juventa of the newly togaed, Fortuna Barbata of grown men now. If I should discourse of the wedding gods: there is Afferenda, properly, of the dowries to be brought; but there are also — for very shame of our offspring! — Mutunus and Tutunus and a goddess Pertunda and Subigus and a goddess Prema and Perfica. Spare us, shameless gods! As the spouses struggle, no one intervenes. They themselves, whose business it is, rejoicing outside, blush.

But he too who affirms us to be priests of the cross will be our fellow-worshipper. The cross's quality is a sign made of wood: you too worship, among your own, wood with an image. Although, just as yours has a human figure, so ours too has its own proper one. Let the outlines now look to themselves, provided the quality is one; let the form look to itself, provided it be the very body of a god. But if a difference comes in here, how much is the Attic Pallas distinguished from the stake of a cross, and the Pharian Ceres, who is represented without form, by a rude stake and a mere shapeless prop of wood? A part of a cross — and indeed the greater part — is every beam fixed in upright position. But to us a whole cross is imputed, with its crossbeam, of course, and with that projection for a seat. In this you are the more inexcusable, who have dedicated a maimed and truncated wood, while others have consecrated it full and complete. For as to the rest, the religion of the whole cross is entire among you, as I shall show. But you do not know that this very origin came to your gods from that gibbet. For every image, whether it is carved from wood or stone, or cast from bronze, or produced from any other richer material, the modeler's hand must first precede it. Now the modeler first sets up a wooden cross, since to our very body too the position is a silent and secret line of a cross. The head juts up, the spine is set straight, the shoulders' slope projects: if you set up a man with hands outspread, you will have made the image of a cross. To this beginning, then, and as it were to this prop, clay woven over it bit by bit completes the limbs, and builds up the body, and packs into the cross the shape that pleases it within the clay; thence, by compass and leaden moulds, the preparation of the image is to be transferred into marble, into mud, or bronze, or whatever it has pleased to be made a god. From the cross, clay; from clay, a god: in a manner the cross passes into the god through the clay. You consecrate the cross, then, from which the consecrated thing takes its beginning. For the sake of example it will be said: from the kernel of an olive, the stone of a peach, and a grain of pepper steeped under the earth, a tree rises into branches, into foliage, into the appearance of its kind. If you transplant it, or use offspring from its branches in another, to what will be assigned what comes from the slip? Not to that grain or stone or kernel? For when the third grade is ascribed to the second, the second is equally ascribed to the first; thus the third will be carried back to the first, transmitted through the second. Nor need we argue longer on this point, since by a natural prescription every kind whatsoever traces its reckoning back to its origin, and the more the kind is reckoned from the origin, so much the more the origin is matched in the kind. If, then, in the kind of gods you worship the cross as origin, here will be the kernel and the primordial grain, from which among you the forests of images are propagated. But here is a thing now manifest. You venerate Victories as deities, and indeed the more august, the more joyous. The construction by which they raise them up — these will be crosses; the trophy is, in a manner, the cross's inner core. And so in the Victories the religion of the camp worships even crosses; it adores the standards, swears by the standards, prefers the standards to Jupiter himself. But that whole array of images, and all that worship of gold, are the necklaces of crosses. So too in the cantabra and the banners, which the soldiery guards with no less sanctity, those streamers are the robes of crosses. You blush, I suppose, to worship crosses unadorned and bare.

And to what length shall I bring forth the gods, since it must be discussed what sort of gods you have received? How much you ought to blush? Whether to laugh at the vanity or to reproach the blindness is quite uncertain. For how many gods, and which, shall I bring forward? The greater or also the lesser? The old or also the recent? The males or also the females? The unwed or also those joined to the bed? The skilled or also the inert? The rustic or also the urban? The citizens or also the foreigners? For so many families, so many nations, in good faith seek the census, that they cannot be looked over and distinguished and described. But the more diffuse the matter is, so much the more must it be straitened by us; and therefore, since in this species we hold to one design — of demonstrating that they were all men (not indeed that you may come to know it, for you act as if forgetful) — let us take a short cut from the very method of looking them over, by retracing the origin of their race. For the origin is of all posterity. That origin of your gods is signed, I suppose, in Saturn. For even if Varro reports the most ancient gods to be Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, it ought not to have escaped us that every father is older than his sons, both Saturn older than Jupiter and Heaven than Saturn; for from Heaven and Earth is Saturn. And yet I pass over the origin of Heaven and Earth. They were, somehow, long unwed and childless before they were husbands and parents. By a long age, of course, they had to grow up to such height. Finally, at the same time the voice began to grow strong in Heaven and the breasts of Earth to harden into pebbles; they make a marriage between themselves. I believe either Heaven came down to the bride, or Earth went up to the bridegroom. At any rate Earth conceived of Heaven, and she bore, in the eighth year, Saturn, by a wondrous reckoning. To which of the parents was he like? But even if she did bear, certainly before Saturn they procreated no one, nor afterwards any but one, Ops; and thereafter there was an end of offspring. For Saturn indeed castrated Heaven as he slept. We read that Heaven is of the masculine gender. But how a father unless masculine? But also, with what was he to be castrated? A sickle for him. At this age, of course? For Vulcan the artificer of iron was not yet. But Earth, bereaved, put off, though still of youthful age, marrying another. But neither did she have another Heaven. Yet what but the Sea embraces her? But it smells of brine; she was used to sweet waters. Thus Saturn the only male of Heaven and Earth. But he himself, coming to manhood, is joined to his own sister. There were not yet laws to forbid incest, nor to punish parricide. And so he devoured his sons of the male sex; he himself was better than the wolves, had he exposed them. He feared, of course, lest any of them should have learned from his father's sickle. Soon, Jupiter being born and stolen away, he gulped down a stone, the feigned infant. By this device long secure, at last, overpowered by the son whom he had not digested, grown up in the darkness, he was deprived of his kingdom. This man, the patriarch of the gods, Heaven and Earth, with the poets as midwives, procreated for you. But some seem to themselves to interpret elegantly, in a physiological way, by allegorical argumentation, that Saturn is Time, and therefore Heaven and Earth his parents, as themselves having no origin, and therefore furnished with a sickle because by time all things are cut apart, and therefore a devourer of his own because all things put forth from himself he consumes back into himself. They call in too the testimony of the name: that he was called in Greek "Kronos" as if "Chronos." Likewise those who conjecture him the procreator deduce the reckoning of the Latin word from sowings, through him the seeds of heaven being borne down into the earth. They join Ops to him, because the seeds confer help ("ops") of living, and again because by labor ("opus") the seeds come forth. What, I pray, is the transference of this — I would have you expound it. Either Saturn was, or Time. How Saturn, if Time? If he, how Time? For you cannot reckon both as corporeal in that one. But what forbade Time to be worshipped in its own quality? What forbade a man's body, or a man's story, to be worshipped in its own species, not in time? What does this notion of yours mean, except to color foul materials with lying argumentations? You neither wish Saturn to be Time, because you say he was a man, nor, while you make him Time, do you any longer wish him to have been a man. Plainly your god Saturn altogether is reviewed, in the records of the ancients, on earth, of human quality. Anything that never existed at all can be feigned incorporeally; there is room for feigning where there is no truth. But since it is settled that Saturn lived, you change him in vain; you are not granted leave concerning one whom you will not deny to have been a man, who can be defended neither as a god nor as Time. The census of Saturn stands everywhere in your literature. We read it in Cassius Severus, in the Cornelii Nepos and Tacitus, among the Greeks too in Diodorus, and whoever else have collected the hoary records of antiquity. Nor are his traces more faithfully marked than in Italy itself. For after very many lands and Attic hospitalities he settled in Italy — or, as it was then called, Oenotria — received by Janus, or Jane, as the Salii call it. The mountain he had inhabited was called Saturnius, the city he marked out is Saturnia to this day; finally all Italy was called from Saturn. With such a witness — the land which now rules the world — even if there is doubt about Saturn's origin, yet about his deeds it is settled that he was a man. Thus, if Saturn was a man, doubtless from a man, nay, because a man, surely not from Heaven and Earth; but, his parents being unknown, it was easy for some to call him the son of gods, of whom all may seem the children. For who would not, for veneration's sake, call heaven and earth father and mother? Or from human custom, by which any unknown persons appearing unexpectedly are said to have come from heaven? Accordingly, because he had come as a stranger, the saying of "heavenly" suddenly grew rooted everywhere. For commonly too we boast that those of uncertain race are sons of the earth. I allege nothing about the state of antiquity, in which both the eyes and minds of men were then so rude that at the sight of any new man they were moved as by something divine — much more of a king, and indeed the first. I shall dwell still on Saturn, that I may build up a short cut for the rest as well, the disputation of beginnings being satisfied; nor shall I pass over the weightier testimonies of the divine writings, to which faith superior for antiquity is owed. For before all literature existed the Sibyl — that Sibyl, I mean, the true prophetess of the true God, from whose name you have clothed the prophets of demons. She, in senarian verse, sets it forth to this sense concerning Saturn's lineage and his affairs: "In the tenth generation of men," she says, "from when the cataclysm befell the former ones, there reigned Saturn and Titan and Iapetus, the mightiest sons of Earth and Heaven." If, then, any faith attaches to your writers or your literature, the older — but for that reason the nearer, since of that age — it has been sufficiently proved concerning Saturn and his lineage that they were men. We hold our short cut, the prescription of origin for the rest, that we may not wander through them one by one. The quality of the posterity is shown from the chiefs of the race: mortal things from mortals, earthly from the earthly; grade is compared to grade; marriages, conceptions, births ran their course; fatherlands, abodes, kingdoms, monuments are plain. Therefore, let those who cannot deny that they were born, believe them dead; let those who confess them dead, not think them gods.

Others, plainly more humanely, suppose the Sun to be the Christian god, because it is known that we make our prayer toward the part of the east, or take our joy on the day of the sun. What of this? Do you do less? Do not most of you, in the affectation of adoring, sometimes even toward the heavenly bodies, move your lips at the rising of the sun? It is you, certainly, who have received the sun into the calendar of the seven days, and have chosen, of those days, the one before it, on which you withhold the bath or put it off till evening, or take your leisure and your dinner. And this indeed you do, straying yourselves, and that from your own to alien religions. For the Jews have their feasts of the sabbaths, and the pure supper, and the Jewish rites of lamps, and fasts with unleavened bread, and prayers on the shore — things which surely are alien from your gods. Wherefore, to return from my digression, you who reproach us with the sun and its day, acknowledge your nearness to us; we are not far from your Saturn and your sabbaths.

But indeed force assists the manifest. Those whom from the beginning they cannot assert to have been anything but men, they receive into divinity, affirming that they were made gods after death, as Varro and those who dreamed with him. Here, then, I take my stand: if your gods have been elected into this name and godhead, as into the senatorial order, you must now of necessity grant — it is your own wisdom — that there is some supreme governor who has the power of electing, and as it were a Caesar; for no one can confer on others what he does not himself rule over. But if they were able to make themselves gods after death, come, why did they choose to be of a worse condition from the beginning? Or if there is no one who has made gods, how shall those be said to have been made who could only have been made by another? Thus no place is given you for refusing that there is a certain proprietor of divinity. Let us, then, examine the causes of electing mortality into heaven. Of these I believe you will produce a twofold reckoning. For either he, whoever so bestowing it acts, does so that he may have supports or defenses or even ornaments of his own height, or the necessity of merits, conferring it upon all the worthy. Anything else you cannot suspect. No one, in bestowing on anyone, acts either not for his own cause or for that one's. But neither can this befit a deity, that, while there is so great a power in him, namely to make gods, so great a humanity should be imposed, that he should need the work or aid of certain persons, and indeed of dead ones — which is a wonder, since from the beginning he could have established immortals for himself. Nor, arguing longer about these things, will he inquire who has compared human things with divine. To be sure, that opinion which is the latter must be examined: whether God has bestowed divinity by the remembrance of merits. But if it was so attributed, if heaven lay open to men of old on account of their merits, it must be reconsidered that thereafter no one was worthy of that honor. Unless the place can no longer hold them. By such great privileges, of course, did antiquity merit the heavenly things. Let us, then, retract whether it merited. He who says it merited, let him set out the merits themselves. If any deeds done in the cradle of temporality avail for the suffrage of divinity, then, defiled with incest, you have received Ops and Saturn as brothers. Your stealthy infant Jupiter, unworthy both of roof and of human breast, deservedly remained in Crete, offspring so bad. Grown up at last, he deprives of his kingdom whatever sort of begetter — most fortunate, the king of the golden age, under whom rested a peace knowing no toil, no want; under whom "no settlers subdued the fields, and the earth herself bore all things, none demanding." But he hated his father, incestuous, and once the castrator of his own grandfather. But behold, he too mingles with his sister, so that I would think that saying first applied to him: "The child takes after the father." As pious a father as a pious son. If even then things were done by just laws, Jupiter ought to have been parted into two sacks. After this, what would he hesitate to do, his lust strengthened by incest, but to spread himself into lighter things, that is, adulteries and debaucheries? Of which poetry has so made sport as we are wont, generally, when something becomes public about a runaway, both to sell his services for another's inquiry and abuse — now figuring him for the prices of luxury, as if he had weighed out an ox or the price of an ox, and sent a shower into the garrets, or burst open an entrance by money; now into the very likenesses of his acts, into the eagle that snatched, the swan that had sung. Are these fables not, then, composed of the most loathsome foulnesses and the highest disgraces? Or do not, perhaps, the manners and characters of men come out the more wanton from them? How these demons, the offspring of evil angels, long since sent forth from faith through unbelief, have striven to turn men aside by similar fables, we need not here treat more at length. For if the same common folk, governed by their kings and princes and propagators, was not indeed of the same nature, yet authority elsewhere demanded a likeness of manners. But how much worse were theirs, who were no better? For by a private title you commonly call Jupiter "the Best," and there is Virgil's "Jove the Just." All alike are incestuous toward their own, unchaste toward strangers, impious, unjust. The one to whom fable has left no signal infamy was not worthy to become a god.

A new report has now been suggested about our god, and not so very recently a certain most abandoned fellow in this city — himself a deserter of his own religion, a Jew only by the loss of his skin, and indeed the more so after the bites of beasts, since he goes about daily to be shaken down over his whole body by those to whom he hires himself — set up a picture against us under this title: "Onocoetes." It had the ears of a pack-mule and was in a toga, with a book, one foot hoofed. And the crowd believed the infamous Jew. For what other kind is there of sowing our infamy? And so throughout the whole city Onocoetes is proclaimed. But this too, as a thing of yesterday, and destitute of the authority of time, and weak from the character of its author, I shall gladly take up in my zeal for turning it back. Let us see, then, whether here too you are caught with us. For it makes no difference under what form, provided we tend to deformed images. There are among you gods with a dog's head, and a lion's, horned with the ox and the ram and the goat, goat-born or serpent-formed, and winged in the foot, the front and the back. Why then do you single out our one? More Onocoetes are caught among you.

But since they would have others received into divinity from men separately, and a distinction made between the born and the made, according to Dionysius the Stoic, I shall add also concerning this species. Of Hercules himself, indeed, will be the sum of the answer, whether he is worthy of heaven and divinity; for thus, at pleasure, they adjudge divinity to merits. If on account of virtue, because he steadfastly dispatched wild beasts, what so memorable? Do not those punished in the games, or even given for the show of the arena's cheapness, dispatch very many at once, and indeed more eager beasts? If on account of traversing the world, to how many, and wealthy ones, sweet liberty, or to philosophers their servile beggary, has done the same? Do they not remember that Asclepiades the Cynic, with a single little cow, on whose back too he was carried and from whose udder, whenever, he was fed, subdued the whole world with his eyes? If Hercules went also to the lower world, who does not know that the road to the lower world lies open to all? If you consecrated him on account of his many slaughters and battles, that great Pompey put forth a far greater number, victor over the pirates of the sea, who had not left even Ostia safe: and how many thousands, I ask, were slain by Scipio in the single corner of the Byrsa of Carthage? So that Scipio is to be reckoned more worthy of divinity than Hercules. Add rather to the Herculean titles the debaucheries of maidens and of wives, and the swaddling-bands of Omphale, and the military service of the Argonauts basely deserted on account of the loss of a comely boy. Add to his glory, after the brand of disgrace, even his furies; adore the arrows that slew his sons and wife. He who would then more worthily have inflicted himself upon the pyre, from grief at his parricides — who, surrounded by poisons on account of his wife's wantonness, deserved rather to die a dishonorable death — him you have lifted up from the pyre into heaven, with that facility by which you raised another too, made away with by the force of divine fire, who, having contrived a few inventions of experience, was said to have recalled the dead to life. He, Apollo's son, as much a man as a grandson of Jupiter, great-grandson of Saturn (or rather a bastard, as of uncertain father, as the Argive Socrates reported, since exposed and found, more basely brought up by Jupiter, namely at a canine udder), deservedly — which no one can deny — was drained off by a thunderbolt. The bad Jupiter is here again "the Best," impious toward his grandson, envious toward the artificer. But indeed Pindar did not conceal his merit: he says that his cupidity and avarice of gain were avenged in him, by which indeed he drove the living to death, but not the dead to life, by the prevarication of venal medicine. His mother too is said to have perished by the same chance, and deservedly she who had brought forth so dangerous a beast for the world burst up to heaven by the same ladder, as it were. And yet the Athenians will know to sacrifice to such gods. For to Aesculapius and his mother they make funeral offerings among the dead. As if they too did not adore their own Theseus, deservedly a god. Why not? If he abandoned his preserver on a foreign shore, by that same forgetfulness, nay madness, which to his father was the cause of death?

If we run together in equality as to the gods, it follows that there is no difference between us as to sacrifice or rite either, so that from another aspect the comparison may be satisfied. We offer or initiate with infanticide. You, if it has slipped your memory what you have done with the slaughter of man and with infanticides, will recognize it in its place; for now we defer many things, lest we seem to be everywhere reviewing the same matters. Meanwhile, as I said, from another quarter there is no lack of equivalence. For though we do it in one way, yet not otherwise are you too infanticides — you who slay your infants once born, forbidden indeed by laws, but no laws are eluded so much, so safely, with the connivance of all, by the tablets of a single age. But it makes no difference even in this, if you slay them not by the rite of sacrifice nor to a god. Indeed, this is the harsher, that you do away with them by cold and famine, or expose them to beasts, or by a longer death drown them in the waters. And if in any way it is done more unlike among you, in this add it: that you extinguish your own offspring, and there will be made up — nay, heaped over — in you whatever has fallen short from another reckoning. But of that sacrifice of impiety we are said to sup. While that too is recognized in you, where it is more conveniently placed, we are not far separated from your voracity. If yours is unchaste, but ours cruel, we are joined, if at all, by nature, in which cruelty always agrees with unchastity. And yet how do you do less — nay, what do you not do more? You gape, of course, too little at human flesh, when you devour the living and the grown? You lap up too little human blood, when you draw out the blood that is to be? You feed too little on the infant, when you drain off the whole infant before its time?

It would be long to review also those whom you have buried among the stars and boldly attended upon as gods. Thus, I suppose, worthy of heaven are the Castors and Perseus and Erigone, just as Jupiter's minion. But what wonder? You have transferred even dogs and scorpions and crabs into heaven. I defer concerning those whom you worship in oracles; this has the testimony of the divine. What? Do you wish the gods to be arbiters even of sorrows, so that there is a Viduus, who widows the soul from the body, whom you have condemned to be shut out by not admitting him within the walls; likewise Caeculus, who deprives the eyes of sense; likewise Orbana, who extinguishes the seed into bereavement; and there is a goddess of death herself. To pass over the rest, you reckon as gods even the places of regions or of the city, Father Janus (and there is a divine Jana of the arches), and Septimontius of the seven mounds. To these same genii they make offerings who have altars or shrines in those places, and besides to others who dwell in another's place or for hire. I say nothing of Ascensus from climbing, and Clivicola from the slopes; I say nothing of the gods Forculus from doors and Cardea from hinges and Limentinus of thresholds, or whatever other doorkeeper deities are adored among you among your neighbors. For what great matter is it, when they have their deities even in brothels, in kitchens, and even in prison? And so heaven is filled with countless proper gods, these and other Roman ones, among whom the offices of the whole of life are distributed, so that there is no need of the other gods. Nay, since those whom we marked above are reckoned privately among the Romans, and not easily known abroad, how do all those things over which they willed them to preside come to pass throughout all the human race and in every nation, where their patrons lack not only honor but even knowledge itself?

We have come to the hour of the lamps and the dogs' service and the contrivances of darkness. At this point I am afraid I may give ground. For what such thing shall I hold against you? But now praise the design of our modest incest, that we have devised an adulterous night, lest we should defile either the light or the true night; that we have thought even the earthly lamps should be spared; that we deceive even our own conscience — for whatever we do, if we wish, we suspect it. But your incests, in their own freedom, enjoy all the light and all the night and the whole consciousness of heaven; and the more happily they come off, since you mingle openly in incest with all heaven conscious of it, you alone are ignorant of it; while we can recognize our crimes even in darkness. Plainly the Persians, as Ctesias relates, live freely with their mothers, as knowing as they are unshuddering. But the Macedonians too — this is what they made plain — openly do it, since, when first the Oedipus of theirs came on the stage, slaughtered as to his eyes, they received him with laughter and derision. The actor, dismayed, drew back his mask: "Surely, masters," he said, "I have not displeased you?" The Macedonians answered: "Nay, you indeed acted beautifully — but either the writer was most foolish, if he made up this, or Oedipus most senseless, if he did it so"; and thereupon one to another said, "Drive on into your mother!" But what little stain is one nation or another upon the whole world? We, indeed, have infected the whole sun, polluted the whole ocean. Give us, then, some nation free of those things that draw the whole human race to incest. If any nation lacks, in intercourse itself and in the necessity of age and sex — not to say in lust and luxury — it will be the one that will lack incest. If any nature is set apart, withdrawn from the human condition, so as to be exposed neither to ignorance nor to error nor to chance, it will be the one that alone can answer more steadfastly to the Christians. Look, then, at lust, fluctuating among errors like the winds, and see whether there are wanting peoples whom the broad shoals and rough places of error drive on to this crime. Above all, when you expose your infants to the mercy of strangers, or for adoption to better parents, do you forget what great matter is supplied for incest, what great occasion is opened to chance? Plainly, the more severe, by some discipline, or with sure regard, restrain such an outcome from lust in whatever place, at home or abroad — so that the scattering of seed and the leaping of lust everywhere may not produce children unknown to you, whom afterwards either the parents themselves or other children may fall upon, since even the moderation of ages is excluded by lust. However many adulteries, however many ravishings, however many wanderings of public lust, whether under a fixed or a roving title — so many minglings of blood, so many compoundings of stock, so many transmissions thence to incest. From this source veins of plots flow to the mimes and comedians; from this source there burst out, like a tragedy, that affair too, judged when Fuscianus was prefect of the City. A boy of noble birth, by the chance carelessness of his attendants, having gone beyond the door, was drawn off by passers-by and lost from his home. A certain little Greek who had reared him — or had snatched him at the very threshold, after the Greek fashion, going in — thence, his age changed, he was brought back from Asia to Rome in the slave-market. The unwitting father bought him and used the Greek; then, as had been the way, the master sent off the youth, grown up, to the country and to chains. There already for a long time the tutor and the nurse were paying their penalty. The whole story is set before them; they tell their fortunes to one another: those, that their nursling had perished in boyhood; he, that he too had perished from boyhood; but with the same outcome, born at Rome of an honorable house; and perhaps he unrolled some marks too. So, then, by the will of God, that so great a stain might be cast in the age's teeth, his breath shook with the day, the times answered with the age, the eyes too recalled something of the features, certain properties in the body were reviewed. The masters — nay, now only the parents — are driven by the diligence of the inquiry brought forward. The slave-dealer is tracked down, unluckily found. The crime revealed, the parents heal themselves with a noose; the prefect assigns the goods to the son who ill survives — not to an inheritance, but to the wages of debauchery and incest. This one example of the public eruption of such crimes lying hidden among you was enough. Nothing happens but once in human affairs. Once, plainly, something can be brought to light from the sacraments of our religion, I suppose. You aim it, and there are matches to it among you, even in things not sacraments.

But indeed some have discovered certain fruits and necessaries of life. I ask you, when you say that they discovered them, do you not confess that the things to be discovered existed before? Why, then, do you not rather honor the author whose gifts these are, but transfer the author to the discoverers? Before he who discovered did so, surely he gave thanks to the author, surely he perceived him a god, whose truly is the ministry of the establisher, by whom both the discoverer himself was established and that very thing which was to be discovered. No one at Rome knew the green African fig when Cato brought it before the senate, to express how near at hand the hostile province now was, which he was always pressing to be subdued. Cnaeus Pompey first published abroad to Italy the cherry from Pontus. The discoverers among the Romans of new fruits could have earned for me the proclamation of divinity. As vain this as also that gods are held on account of the inventions of the arts. With whom if the artificers of our age were compared, how much more worthily would consecration have befitted the later than the earlier? I ask you, has not antiquity by now been outgrown in all crafts, since daily use everywhere equips novelty? And so those whom you sanctify on account of their arts, you injure in the very arts, and you provoke them with rivals who surpass them.

As for your charges of obstinacy or presumption, if you bring any forward, not even these withdraw from the fellowship of comparison. The first obstinacy is that which is set up as second to religion toward God — the obstinacy of Caesar's majesty: that we are called irreligious toward the Caesars, neither propitiating their images nor swearing by their genii. We are named enemies of the people. So be it, indeed — since out of you, nations, there are daily made Caesars Parthian and Median and German. On this point let the Roman race see in what manner the untamed and foreign nations stand. You, however, from among our own, conspire against our own. We acknowledge, to be sure, the Roman fidelity toward the Caesars. No conspiracy ever broke out, no blood of a Caesar in the senate or in the very palaces ever fixed a brand, no majesty was aimed at in the provinces. As yet the Syrias reek with the odors of corpses; as yet the Gauls do not wash in their own Rhone. But I pass over the crimes of madness, since even these the Roman name does not admit. The sacrileges of vanity I will deal with, and recognize the irreverence of your very home-bred race — both the festive lampoons that the statues know, and those words sometimes hurled aslant, with curses, by the assembly, that resound through the circus. If not in arms, at least in tongue you are always rebels. But it is one thing, I suppose, not to swear by the genius of Caesar — for one is in doubt about perjury's right, since not even by your gods do you swear in good faith. But we do not call the emperor a god; for upon this, when the crowd says so, we make a wry face. Nay, rather, you who call Caesar a god both mock him, by saying what he is not, and curse him, because he does not wish to be what you say. For he would rather live than become a god.

Finally, you do not deny to the patrons of your religion all those whom antiquity willed to be gods, posterity believed. There remains to us still that very great presumption of the Roman superstitions, with which, against you, nations, we have to engage: namely, that the Romans were made lords and arbiters of the whole world for this reason, that by the offices of religions they deserved so to rule, that it is little short of their prevailing over their very own gods. Doubtless Sterculus and Mutunus and Larentina advanced this empire. The Romans alone, the people destined by their own gods to dominion. For I would not think that they wished it done rather for a foreign people than for their own — that they should become deserters and abandoners, nay, betrayers of their native soil, in which they were born, grew up, were ennobled and buried. Thus not even Jupiter would allow his own Crete to be shaken by the Roman fasces, forgetful of that Idaean cave and the Corybantian bronze and the most pleasant odor of his nurse there. Would he not have preferred that tomb of his to every Capitol, that rather that land should reign which covered Jupiter's ashes? Would Juno have wished the Punic city — beloved before Samos — to be consumed, of all things, by the fires of the Aeneadae? Though I know that "here were her arms, here her chariot; that this should be a kingdom for the nations, the goddess even then, if by any means the fates allow, strives and cherishes." Wretched, she did not prevail against the fates! And yet the Romans decreed not so much honor to the fates that, when they surrendered Carthage to themselves, they gave as much as to Larentina. But these gods are not in the power of conferring a kingdom. For if Jupiter reigned in Crete and Saturn in Italy and Isis in Egypt, men too have reigned, to whom indeed many are reported to have done service. Thus he who serves both makes lords, and the surrendered slave of Admetus increases the Roman citizens with empire, while he ruined his liberal worshipper Croesus by deceiving him with ambiguous oracles. What did the god fear, steadfastly to foretell that his kingdom must fall from him? Increased with the power of reigning, could they ever even have protected their own cities! If they were able to bestow on the Romans, why did Minerva not defend Athens from Xerxes? Or why did Apollo not rescue Delphi from the hand of Pyrrhus? They guard the city of Rome who lost their own — if this is what Roman religiosity has merited. But was not superstition sought after, when the supreme empire was already attained, things now increased? Even if rites were introduced by Numa, yet not yet by images or temples did they delude your affairs with the divine. Frugal was the religion and poverty-stricken the superstition; the altars rude and the vessels mean, and small the smoke from them, and the god himself nowhere. Therefore they were not religious before they were great, because religious. Then how can it seem that empire was sought for the Romans on account of supreme religion and the deepest care of the gods, when it was increased rather by the gods being injured? For unless I am mistaken, every kingdom or empire is sought by wars and enlarged by wars. Moreover, in victories the very gods of a city are injured. For there is the same destruction both of walls and of temples, equal slaughters both of citizens and of priests, the same plunderings of profane things and of sacred. As many sacrileges of the Romans as trophies, as many triumphs thereafter over gods as over nations. There remain too captive images, and surely, if they perceive their conquerors, they do not love them. But because they perceive nothing, they are injured with impunity, and because they are injured with impunity, they are adored in vain. And so those whose height has grown up through victories cannot be seen to have increased by the merits of religion, having increased either as injurers of religion in growing, or by injuring. A kingdom all nations have had, each in its own times, as the Assyrians, as the Medes, as the Persians, as the Egyptians; it is even now with certain peoples, and yet those who have lost it did not dwell without religions and worship and the gods made propitious, until at last almost the whole dominion passed to the Romans. The lot of the times has so rolled the kingdoms. Seek who has ordained the changes of the times. The same dispenses the kingdoms, and now, among the Romans, has gathered that sum, as it were money exacted from many names, into one chest. What he has decreed about it, they know who are nearest to him.

The remainder of obstinacy you place under this head: that we refuse with our minds neither your swords nor crosses nor beasts, not fire, not tortures, on account of our hardness and contempt of death. But indeed all these things, among your elders and forefathers, learned not only to be despised but even to be weighed with great praise from virtue. The sword — how many and how great men, of their own will! It is irksome to recount. The cross's novelty, frequent, abstruse, your own Regulus gladly dedicated; the queen of Egypt used her own beasts; the fires, after the Carthaginian woman more steadfast than her husband Hasdrubal in her country's last extremities, Dido herself had taught men to brave. But tortures too the Attic woman wearied, denying the tyrant, and at the last, lest her body and sex should give way, spat out her own tongue, having chewed it — the whole instrument of confession rooted out. But these things in your people you reckon to glory, in ours to hardness. Destroy now the glory of your forefathers, that you may destroy us too. Be content to detract even from the praise of your parents for the present, lest you give us a place from these examples. Perhaps the very quality of the times of a sturdier antiquity demanded harder spirits. But now, in the tranquility of peace, both spirits are softer and the minds of men are milder even toward strangers. "Be it so," you say; "compare yourselves with the ancients; for us it is needful to pursue with hatred, in you, what is not approved by us, because it is not even found in us." Answer, then, to each particular. I do not demand examples in the same voice. If, of course, contempt of death made tales of the sword among your forefathers, surely it is not from love of life that you hire yourselves out by the sword to the trainers, that from fear of death you give your names to military service. If for some woman there is a famous death from beasts, in the midst of peace, daily, of your own free will, you go to the beasts. If no Regulus among you has yet engaged with the cross, the machine for fixing the body, yet by now the contempt of fire has come about, since one of you recently hired himself out, to be clothed in the fiery tunic, up to a fixed place throughout. If a woman insulted the scourges, this too one of you recently, in the hunters' ranks, after running through his round, has measured out again — to say nothing of the Laconian glory.

Thus far, I suppose, the horrors of Christian obstinacies. If we share these with you, it remains to compare the persons to be derided. Although all our obstinacy is built up beforehand from persuasions; for we presume the resurrection of the dead. The hope of resurrection is a disdain of death. Laugh, then, as much as you please at the most stupid minds, which die that they may live; but, that you may laugh the more easily and break out in the more unrestrained guffaws, snatch up a sponge or, for the moment, your tongue, and blot out for the moment your own writings, which likewise assert that souls will return into bodies. Yet how much more acceptable is our presumption, which maintains that they will return into the same bodies! But to you how much more empty a thing has been handed down — that a man's spirit will return in a dog or a mule or a peacock? Likewise we announce a judgment appointed by God, according to each one's merits, after death. This you ascribe to Minos and Rhadamanthus, the juster Aristides being meanwhile rejected. By that judgment we say that the unjust will pass eternity in eternal fire, the pious and innocent in a place of delight. Among you too the condition of Pyriphlegethon and Elysium is disposed in no other way. Nor do the mythic and the poets alone sing such things, but the philosophers too affirm the reciprocation of souls and the distribution of judgment.

How long, then, most unjust nations, will you not acknowledge — nay, more, will you execrate your own kind — if there is no difference between us, if we are one and the same? Since you do not hate what you are, rather give us your right hands, join in kisses, mingle embraces, the bloody with the bloody, the incestuous with the incestuous, the conspirators with the conspirators, the obstinate and vain with your equals. We have injured the divine powers of the gods alike, we provoke their indignation alike. You too have a third race, though not of a third rite, yet of a third sex. That is more fitly joined of man and woman, with men and women. Or is it perhaps by our very fellowship that we offend you? Equality is wont to supply the matter of rivalry. Thus potter envies potter, smith smith. Nay, by now have done with your feigned confession! Conscience has returned to truth and to the steadfastness of truth. For all these things are present in us alone, and are refuted by us alone against whom they are brought — namely, by the recognition of the opposite party, whence, knowledge being equipped, it inspires counsel and governs judgment. Your own verdict, finally, is that no one should judge a case unless both sides are heard, which in our case alone you neglect. You satisfy nature's fault, condemning in others what you do not refute in yourselves, or casting upon others the guilt that you remember in yourselves. You will be occupied with diverse work: chaste toward strangers, incestuous toward yourselves; more vigorous abroad, subdued at home. This is the injustice — that we should be judged by the knowing from the ignorant, the acquitted from the guilty. Take the beam from your own eye, that you may draw the mote from another's. Amend yourselves first, that you may punish the Christians. Unless you amend, you will not punish; nay, you will be Christians; nay, if you become Christians, you will be amended. Learn what you accuse in us, and you will not accuse; recognize what you do not accuse in yourselves, and you will accuse. From this point it now lies open to you, so far as we have been able to open it in these few little books, both the inspection of error and the recognition of truth. Condemn the truth — but only when inspected, if you can; and approve error — but only when discovered, if you think so. But if it is prescribed for you to love error and to hate truth, why do you not come to know what you love and what you hate?
